cond.rhinitis.name: Allergic rhinitis
cond.gastroenteritis.name: Gastroenteritis
cond.heartburn.name: Acid reflux (heartburn)
cond.musclePain.name: Muscle pain & lower back pain
cond.rash.name: Hives & skin rash
cond.conjunctivitis.name: Conjunctivitis (pink eye)
cond.toothache.name: Toothache & gum inflammation
cond.uti.name: Bladder infection (cystitis)
cond.stress.name: Stress, insomnia & low mood
cond.cold.summary: A common viral infection of the nose and throat. Most people get better on their own within 1–2 weeks; medicine helps ease the symptoms.
cond.flu.summary: Infection with the influenza virus causes a sudden high fever, chills, and severe body aches. If you see a doctor within 48 hours of the symptoms starting, you can ask about an antiviral prescription.
cond.covid19.summary: Infection with the COVID-19 virus. Fever, cough, and sore throat are common, and you can buy a self-test kit at a pharmacy. If you are short of breath or have a chronic illness, see a doctor.
cond.rhinitis.summary: An allergy to things like pollen, dust, or dust mites that causes repeated sneezing, a clear runny nose, a stuffy nose, and itchy eyes. It usually doesn't cause a fever.
cond.gastroenteritis.summary: A virus or spoiled food inflames the intestines, causing diarrhea, vomiting, and stomach pain. The most important thing is to replace enough water and electrolytes.
cond.indigestion.summary: Your upper belly feels full and bloated and food doesn't digest well, often from overeating, greasy food, or stress.
cond.heartburn.summary: Stomach acid comes up into the esophagus, causing a burning feeling in the chest or a sour taste coming up. Late-night meals, alcohol, and greasy food are common causes.
cond.headache.summary: Tension headaches are the most common, caused by lack of sleep, stress, eye strain, or dehydration. If one side throbs and you become sensitive to light and sound, it may be a migraine.
cond.musclePain.summary: Pain from muscles or ligaments strained by too much exercise or by staying in the same position for a long time. Most cases get better within a few days to a few weeks.
cond.menstrualCramps.summary: Your lower belly and lower back hurt around the start of your period. Painkillers work best if you take them early, when the pain starts.
cond.rash.summary: Skin gets red, swollen, or itchy for many reasons, such as food, medicine, insects, sweat, or infection. Try to remember if you recently started any new medicine or food.
cond.conjunctivitis.summary: Inflammation of the membrane covering the white of the eye causes redness, itching, and eye discharge. The viral type spreads easily, so handwashing is important.
cond.toothache.summary: Tooth decay or gum inflammation makes teeth sensitive or painful, and gums may swell or bleed. Painkillers only ease the pain for a while, so you need to see a dentist.
cond.constipation.summary: Stools are hard and you go less often. Common causes are a change of environment, not enough water or fiber, and lack of exercise.
cond.uti.summary: Usually bacteria get into the bladder, so it stings when you pee and you need to go often. You may need antibiotics, so it's best to see a doctor.
cond.hangover.summary: Headache, nausea, and tiredness after drinking alcohol. Taking acetaminophen (paracetamol, e.g., Tylenol) for a hangover can put a strain on your liver.
cond.stress.summary: A new environment, a new language, and study pressure can lead to trouble sleeping, or anxiety or low mood that doesn't go away. Don't struggle alone; it's okay to ask for help.
care.rest: Get plenty of rest and sleep.
care.fluids: Drink water often, a little at a time.
care.humidify: Keep your room warm and humid.
care.mask: Wear a mask when you're around other people.
care.isolate: Skip classes and gatherings until your fever is gone, and keep your distance from others.
care.selfTest: You can buy a self-test kit at a pharmacy and test yourself.
care.avoidTriggers: Avoid your triggers (pollen, dust, certain foods).
care.salineRinse: Rinse your nose with saline solution.
care.oralRehydration: Drink an oral rehydration solution (electrolyte drink) sold at pharmacies.
care.lightMeals: Start with soft foods like rice porridge, bananas, and plain white rice.
care.avoidLateMeals: Don't eat in the 2–3 hours before bed.
care.avoidAlcohol: Cut down on alcohol, caffeine, and greasy or spicy food.
care.screenBreak: When looking at screens for a long time, rest your eyes often.
care.coldCompress: For the first 1–2 days after an injury, apply ice.
care.stretch: When the pain eases, stretch gently and keep moving.
care.avoidScratch: Don't scratch; keep the area cool.
care.lukewarmShower: Wash with lukewarm water instead of hot water.
care.eyeHygiene: Don't rub your eyes, and use your own towel.
care.noContacts: Don't wear contact lenses until it heals.
care.dentalHygiene: Brush with a soft toothbrush and use dental floss.
care.fiberWater: Get plenty of fiber, like vegetables and fruit, and plenty of water.
care.exercise: Move your body every day, for example with a light walk.
care.noHolding: Don't hold in your pee for a long time.
care.sleepRoutine: Go to bed and get up at the same time every day.
care.talkSomeone: Talk to someone you trust or to the school counseling center.
flag.breathing: It's hard to breathe, or my lips are turning blue
flag.chestPain: Pressing chest pain that won't go away
flag.confusion: I feel confused or foggy, or can't understand what people say
flag.worstHeadache: A sudden headache, the worst I've ever had
flag.weakness: My arm or leg on one side feels weak, or my speech is slurred
flag.facialSwelling: My lips, face, or throat are swelling and it's hard to breathe
flag.bloodStoolVomit: Vomiting blood, or black or bloody stool
flag.severeAbdomen: My belly is hard and the pain is unbearable
flag.headInjury: Vomiting or constantly sleepy after hitting my head
flag.selfHarm: I'm having thoughts of hurting myself
flag.heavyBleeding: Bleeding won't stop, or I soak through a pad every hour
flag.visionLoss: Suddenly I can't see well, or my eye hurts badly
flag.pregnancyPain: I could be pregnant and have severe lower belly pain or bleeding
flag.stiffNeckFever: Fever with a stiff neck, so it's hard to bend my head forward
flag.numbnessWeakness: My legs feel numb and weak, or I can't control my bladder or bowels
flag.highFever: A fever of 39℃ or higher that lasts more than 3 days, even with fever reducers
flag.dehydration: I'm barely peeing and feel dizzy, or I can't even drink water
flag.longLasting: Not better after more than 10 days, or getting better and then worse again
flag.spreadingRedness: A red area keeps spreading and feels hot, or has pus
flag.flankFever: Pain in my side (flank) with fever and chills
flag.swellingFever: My face or jaw is swollen and I have a fever
caution.alcoholLiver: It can damage your liver if you drink alcohol that day or drink every day.
caution.maxDose: Do not take more than the maximum daily dose.
caution.duplicate: Check that your cold medicine and painkillers don't contain the same ingredient.
caution.stomach: It may upset your stomach. Don't take it on an empty stomach; take it with food.
caution.drowsy: It may make you drowsy. Avoid driving or dangerous work.
caution.pregnancy: If you're pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to a pharmacist or doctor first.
caution.children: Children have separate products and doses.
caution.bloodPressure: If you have high blood pressure, heart disease, or thyroid disease, talk to a pharmacist or doctor first.
caution.caffeine: It contains caffeine, so it may make it hard to sleep.
caution.shortTerm: If you're not better after using it for a few days, see a doctor.
caution.externalOnly: This medicine goes on the skin (cream or patch). Do not eat or swallow it.
caution.steroidLong: Do not use it on your face or on large areas for a long time.
caution.infectiousDiarrhea: If you have a high fever or bloody diarrhea, do not take it; see a doctor.
caution.separateDose: Take it about 2 hours apart from other medicines.
caution.asthmaNsaid: Do not take it if aspirin or anti-inflammatory painkillers have ever given you asthma or hives.
caution.kidney: If you have kidney disease, talk to a pharmacist or doctor first.
caution.reye: Do not use it for colds or flu in children or teenagers.
caution.sunlight: Keep the skin where the patch was out of the sun for a while, even after you take it off.
caution.washHands: Wash your hands after applying it, and don't touch your eyes with those hands.

campus.title: Campus life & first visit
campus.firstVisit: Going to a clinic for the first time
campus.step.book: Check if you need an appointment
campus.step.book.body: Most small clinics take walk-ins without an appointment. Large hospitals may need one, so call first.
campus.step.book.say: Can I see a doctor today? Do I need an appointment?
campus.step.bring.body: Bring your residence card (ARC) or passport, proof of health insurance, the medicines you're taking, and your symptom card.
campus.step.bring.say: Can I check in with my residence card (ARC)?
campus.step.reception.body: At the front desk, say it's your first visit and show your symptom card. You may get a form to fill in your personal details.
campus.step.reception.say: It's my first time here. I'd like to see a doctor.
campus.step.consult.body: When they call your name, go into the doctor's room. If you didn't understand something, it's okay to ask them to say it again.
campus.step.pay.body: Pay the fee, and get the receipt and the itemized statement of charges you need for insurance claims.
campus.step.pay.say: Please give me a receipt and an itemized statement of the charges.
campus.step.pharmacy.body: If you got a prescription, take it to a nearby pharmacy. Make sure you know how to take the medicine.
campus.step.pharmacy.say: Please tell me slowly how to take this medicine.
